title: Trespass to land is direct and unlawful interference with possession

content.overview: Trespass to land is direct and unlawful interference with possession. Trespass ab initio concerns abuse of a lawful entry authority; jus tertii is the limited rule concerning a stranger's superior title.
content.glance: Trespass to land is direct and unlawful interference with possession. Trespass ab initio concerns abuse of a lawful entry authority; jus tertii is the limited rule concerning a stranger's superior title.
content.study: Trespass to land is direct and unlawful interference with possession. Trespass ab initio concerns abuse of a lawful entry authority; jus tertii is the limited rule concerning a stranger's superior title.\n\nTrespass protects possession rather than abstract title. Entick v Carrington illustrates strict protection against unauthorised entry; the Six Carpenters' Case developed trespass ab initio.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Trespass protects possession rather than abstract title. Entick v Carrington illustrates strict protection against unauthorised entry; the Six Carpenters' Case developed trespass ab initio.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: The action is common-law and may be affected by statutory authority, licence, easement, necessity or consent. The claimant generally relies on possession and direct interference.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Possession or protected interest. 2. Direct entry, remaining or placing an object. 3. No authority or consent. 4. Causal connection. Substantial damage is not necessary for liability.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Survey plans, possession records, photographs, witness testimony and admissions may prove boundaries and entry.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Ordinary claims are civil. Injunction and possession remedies may accompany damages. Limitation depends on relief and statute.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Trespass protects possession against direct unauthorised interference; a stranger's title is not a general justification.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Possession can support trespass liability even where title is not absolute.

distinctions.title: Trespass vs Nuisance
distinctions.left: Trespass to Land, Trespass Ab Initio & Jus Tertii
distinctions.right: Trespass is direct interference with possession; nuisance generally concerns interference with use or enjoyment.
